summary: The developer machine has the tools and DocumentDB MCP server needed to implement the Node.js + Mongoose sample and verify indexes/queries against the live Azure DocumentDB cluster. Most model (cold) answers were outdated or confused with Azure Cosmos DB (MongoDB API) or other neighbours; these are documented and corrected. Missing CLI tools (mongosh) and some optional accelerators are not blocking but would speed verification. One unresolved info gap remains about a recommended Mongoose package version for MongoDB wire protocol 7/8 compatibility.
summary_points: Build can start: Node.js, npm/npx, Docker, Azure CLI, documentdb MCP server and the DocumentDB-specific skills are present and usable for code and verification.

Several cold answers were wrong/outdated — the service uses Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters, an az documentdb CLI group, vCore compute tiers (M30 etc.), SRV-style cluster hostnames (.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com), integrated vector and text search, and change streams — not the Cosmos RU model or older Cosmos DB account APIs.
Missing but non-blocking items: mongosh is not on PATH (handy for local checks) and the DocumentDB Agent Kit accelerator is not installed; both speed development and verification.
Information gap: explicit recommended Mongoose version for Node.js 24 targeting MongoDB wire protocol 7/8 was not found in the docs searched.

Verdict is ready_with_gaps because all required pieces to build and verify the sample are available, but the builder should follow the corrected facts below and may install optional tools to ease manual verification.

tools.name: node
tools.needed_for: Run the sample service, npm scripts, install packages, and run local test/seed scripts.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run or build the Node.js service.
tools.workaround: Install Node.js 24 from nodejs.org; use Docker container with Node if install is not possible.

tools.name: npx / npm
tools.needed_for: Install dependencies, run seed scripts, and start MCP-related tooling if needed.
tools.detail: npx 11.19.0 (npm implied via Node), npm available
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run npm install / npm scripts or launch utility npm-based tooling.
tools.workaround: Install Node.js (which includes npm) or run inside a Node Docker image.

tools.name: documentdb
tools.needed_for: Data-plane verification (list databases/collections, create/list indexes, run explain/aggregate, insert/test data).
tools.detail: MCP server 'documentdb' available with 18 tools (list/create indexes, aggregate, explain, find, insert, etc.) - requires connection_profile "default"
tools.impact_if_missing: Builder couldn't inspect the live cluster, confirm indexes, sample documents, or run explains — would block verification against the real cluster.
tools.workaround: Use mongosh or driver-based checks to inspect the cluster; however the documentdb MCP toolkit provides convenience and authoritative checks.

tools.name: learn (Microsoft Learn docs MCP)
tools.needed_for: Ground facts about resource types, CLI commands, connection strings, vector/search features, and other service behavior.
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to verify or ground current product documentation; increased risk of using outdated model memory.
tools.workaround: Fall back to web browser / saved docs, or rely on installed skill guidance.

tools.name: az (Azure CLI)
tools.needed_for: Inspect cluster resource in Azure, get connection strings from Azure resource, create firewall rules (if required), and run az documentdb commands if needed.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot read cluster resource properties or connection-strings from the control plane; harder to script cluster-side checks.
tools.workaround: Use the Azure portal to view connection strings and settings; use the documentdb MCP server for data-plane tasks.

tools.name: docker
tools.needed_for: Run local DocumentDB gateway image for local integration testing (optional).
tools.impact_if_missing: Can't run local DocumentDB gateway container for local dev; must test against live cluster.
tools.workaround: Test against the live cluster provided (DOCUMENTDB_URI), or use a remote test cluster.

references.title: Development loop - run DocumentDB in Docker

tools.name: mongosh
tools.needed_for: Manual connectivity checks, direct index inspection, ad-hoc queries during development/verification.
tools.impact_if_missing: Loss of quick ad-hoc shell verification convenience; can still use documentdb MCP server or driver-based checks in Node to inspect cluster.
tools.workaround: Use the documentdb MCP server tools (documentdb_find_documents, documentdb_list_indexes, documentdb_explain_operation) or a small Node script using the MongoDB driver / Mongoose to run the same checks.

references.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using MongoDB Shell

tools.name: git
tools.needed_for: Source control, creating the sample repo and committing code.
tools.impact_if_missing: Can't version or publish sample code from this machine.
tools.workaround: Use compressed archive or manual file transfer.

tools.name: documentdb-driver (skill)
tools.needed_for: Guidance on correct MongoClient/Mongoose patterns for Azure DocumentDB (singleton client, connection options, pooling).
tools.impact_if_missing: Less guidance on driver-specific best practices (connection pooling, timeouts) and more risk of connection misconfiguration.
tools.workaround: Follow generic MongoDB/Mongoose docs and the documentdb-connection skill.

tools.name: documentdb-connection (skill)
tools.needed_for: Tune Mongoose/MongoClient connection pools, timeouts and TLS behavior for DocumentDB cluster.
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to correctly tune connection options for the sample; may lead to connection timeouts or pool exhaustion during seed/load runs.
tools.workaround: Use default driver settings or consult online docs; avoid high parallel writes during seed.

tools.name: documentdb-indexing (skill)
tools.needed_for: Advice on declaring and choosing indexes (compound, multikey, vector/text) and ensuring index create semantics for DocumentDB.
tools.impact_if_missing: Less precise guidance on which index shapes to use; risk of inefficient queries.
tools.workaround: Create the two required compound indexes as specified by the prompt and use the documentdb MCP server to verify with explain.

tools.name: documentdb-local-deployment (skill)
tools.needed_for: Instructions for running a local DocumentDB gateway container (port 10260) for local development if the builder prefers a local dev DB.
tools.impact_if_missing: Less guidance on local dev setup; but not required because live cluster is provided.
tools.workaround: Use the live cluster provided via DOCUMENTDB_URI for integration tests.

tools.name: documentdb-vector-search (skill)
tools.needed_for: If the sample adds vector fields or demonstrates vector search, this skill explains creating DiskANN/HNSW/IVF indexes and the $search stage.
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to implement vector search examples; but vector search is optional for this sample.
tools.workaround: Omit vector features or follow the docs linked in the report.

accelerators_missed: DocumentDB Agent Kit (accelerator): not installed; would speed sample generation and include more opinionated templates and scripts. Install with: npx skills add Azure/documentdb-agent-kit

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type for an account/cluster: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts
confusions.grounded_answer: The current resource type for an Azure DocumentDB (MongoDB-compatible vCore) cluster is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts).

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters 2024-07-01 (deployment-language-terraform)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Shared provider namespace and historical overlap: older Cosmos DB accounts used Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts for Cosmos DB resources; the new vCore product uses a distinct resource type (mongoClusters) under the same provider namespace.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore) cluster `[Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters]`

confusions.build_risk: Using databaseAccounts would cause an IaC or az CLI attempt to deploy or inspect the wrong resource type, or an az/curl call to fail when trying to manage mongoClusters resources. Automation using the wrong resource type will not find or create the expected cluster.
improvements: Add a clear note on the 'Quickstart' pages that 'Azure DocumentDB' clusters are deployed as Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (link to templates/mongoclusters).
On any page that still references Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts for MongoDB, add a deprecation/clarification that the new vCore clusters use mongoClusters.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the built-in core CLI group az cosmosdb (e.g. az cosmosdb create / az cosmosdb show / az cosmosdb keys list). This is part of the core az CLI (no separate extension required for basic account management).
confusions.grounded_answer: The correct command group for the vCore DocumentDB clusters is az documentdb (and az documentdb mongocluster create / show / list-connection-strings). There is/was an az cosmosdb mongocluster group in some docs, but az documentdb is the canonical group for the managed mongoClusters resource and the az documentdb CLI extension is used for some preview commands.

grounding_links.title: az documentdb mongocluster create
Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The older Cosmos DB MongoDB API used az cosmosdb commands; the newer Azure DocumentDB vCore product uses an az documentdb command group (documentdb CLI extension). Same 'cosmos' / 'documentdb' naming area caused confusion.
confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb commands may fail to target the vCore resource or return unexpected outputs; scripts that call the wrong CLI group will not find cluster connection strings or manipulate the intended resource.
improvements: Add a cross-link and short note on the az cosmosdb CLI pages and the Quickstart that for vCore-based managed MongoDB the az documentdb group (az documentdb mongocluster) is the primary CLI surface.
Document clearly in the CLI quickstart that az documentdb is the command group for DocumentDB (mongoClusters).

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts; Terraform: azurerm_cosmosdb_account with kind 'MongoDB'.
confusions.grounded_answer: For the vCore Azure DocumentDB cluster the correct resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (Bicep/ARM templates) and Terraform should target the relevant Azure resource (templates or AzAPI/AzureRM AVM modules that deploy Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters). azurerm_cosmosdb_account is for Cosmos DB account resources (older model) and is not the canonical resource for mongoClusters.

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (deployment-language-bicep)
Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters 2024-07-01 (deployment-language-terraform)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB-based MongoDB examples and Terraform modules use azurerm_cosmosdb_account; the new vCore product uses a distinct ARM resource type (mongoClusters).
confusions.build_risk: Using the databaseAccounts / azurerm_cosmosdb_account type would create or try to manage the wrong resource, and automated IaC or examples would not target the actual mongoClusters resource the cluster uses.
improvements: Add an explicit 'use mongoClusters' migration note on the Terraform/Bicep quickstarts and AVM module pages so authors pick the right resource type.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@<account>@ (or SRV form mongodb+srv://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com/...). Key requirements: TLS=true, replicaSet=globaldb, port 10255.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB vCore clusters provide SRV-style hostnames and connection strings like mongodb+srv://<username>@<cluster-name>.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?tls=true&authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256&retrywrites=false (portal and az documentdb list-connection-strings). The host suffix and parameters differ from older Cosmos DB (which used .mongo.cosmos.azure.com and port 10255). Use the portal or az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings to retrieve the correct URI.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using Azure portal
az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings
Connect to Azure DocumentDB from Azure Databricks (shows SRV example)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The older Cosmos DB for MongoDB API used hostnames like .mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255 and required replicaSet=globaldb; DocumentDB vCore uses a distinct host suffix (.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com) and SRV patterns. Shared terms ('mongo', 'cosmos', 'DocumentDB') cause overlap.

confusion_sources.title: Cosmos DB MongoDB connection string docs (older)

confusions.build_risk: Passing the wrong host/port/params to Mongoose would cause connection failures or misconfiguration (TLS/auth failures). Scripts that hardcode port 10255 or replicaSet=globaldb will fail to connect to the vCore cluster or use incorrect options.
improvements: Add explicit SRV vs direct connection examples in the DocumentDB quickstarts and a 'How to craft DOCUMENTDB_URI' snippet for Node/Mongoose on the quickstart page.
Add a short note in the 'connect' docs clarifying the difference from older cosmos.mongo examples and that az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings is the authoritative source.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Capacity is billed in Request Units (RUs) for the Cosmos DB/MongoDB API. You provision throughput as RU/s at the account/database/collection level (or use autoscale RU).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore) is billed by compute tier (vCores) and storage (you pick M30, M40, etc.), not RUs. There are no per-operation RU charges for this product; compute (vCores) and storage are billed independently.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB pricing explained
Compute and storage configurations for Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Old Cosmos DB (MongoDB API) uses RU-based billing; the new vCore DocumentDB product uses tiered vCore billing. Shared naming around DocumentDB/Cosmos caused the mix-up.
confusions.build_risk: If a builder assumed RU-based quotas they might attempt to tune or provision throughput in the wrong way or use autoscale/RU APIs that don't apply to vCore clusters.
improvements: Add a short 'pricing model' banner at the top of the quickstart and migration pages that clearly contrasts the vCore (compute+storage) vs RU models.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: For the MongoDB API you normally authenticate with the MongoDB username/password credentials (Cosmos DB database users / account keys exposed as connection strings). Cosmos DB data-plane also supports primary/master keys and resource tokens for management. Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) integrated authentication is available for the Cosmos DB SQL API in certain scenarios, but typical MongoDB drivers use SCRAM username/password via the URI. There is not a widely-used Azure AD token flow for MongoDB drivers in most Cosmos accounts (use the connection string credentials).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports Native (username/password, SCRAM) authentication and Microsoft Entra ID (RBAC) authentication for data-plane access. The service exposes the ability to use Azure AD identities and managed identities (passwordless workflows) for data-plane access when RBAC/Entra ID is enabled; documentation shows how to enable Microsoft Entra ID auth and how to acquire role-based credentials for the cluster. Native credentials remain supported for most drivers and are commonly used in samples.

grounding_links.title: Connect a Node.js application - notes on Microsoft Entra ID authentication
Connect to Azure DocumentDB using Azure portal (passwordless / Microsoft Entra ID guidance)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB MongoDB API docs historically emphasized username/password and resource tokens; the newer vCore DocumentDB product added/enabled Microsoft Entra ID data-plane modes and passwordless patterns, which the cold answer overlooked.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes Azure AD is not supported they may over-share credentials (store password in repo) instead of using managed identities or RBAC where available.
improvements: Add a short how-to snippet in the Node/Mongoose quickstart showing both native (SCRAM) and Microsoft Entra ID/passwordless connection examples and how to enable RBAC in the portal.

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: As I understand Cosmos DB's MongoDB API does not provide built-in vector-index types like HNSW/IVF/DiskANN in the MongoDB wire protocol. There is no native command to create a vector index via the MongoDB createIndex API in Cosmos DB.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB includes an integrated vector store and supports vector index kinds: vector-ivf, vector-hnsw, and vector-diskann. Indexes are created via the createIndexes-style command including a 'cosmosSearchOptions' (or 'kind' parameter) and then the $search aggregation stage (cosmosSearch) is used to query vectors. DiskANN/HNSW/IVF are explicitly supported and documented.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB
Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (DiskANN, HNSW, IVF examples)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer describes older Cosmos DB limitations (or other MongoDB-hosted services) that lacked integrated vector indexes; Azure DocumentDB (vCore) includes built-in vector indexes.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes vector indexes are unavailable they may choose a separate vector DB or omit the integrated search features; not critical for this sample unless vector search is added.
improvements: Document examples of createIndexes + cosmosSearch (HNSW/IVF/DiskANN) on the quickstarts and show a Node snippet to create and query a vector index.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Full-text or hybrid search is done by integrating Cosmos DB with Azure Cognitive Search (Azure Search) or by using Cosmos DB's search integration (if your account has the integrated search feature enabled). For MongoDB API customers the usual pattern is to index/copy data into Azure Cognitive Search and run full-text queries there, or use an external search engine.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB provides built-in full-text and hybrid search via createSearchIndexes and the $search aggregation stage (cosmosSearch). Hybrid search (lexical + vector) and BM25-style full-text features are supported through the integrated search features and the $search stage; external Azure Cognitive Search is not required for these features.

grounding_links.title: Full-text and hybrid search using createSearchIndexes and $search

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Many Cosmos DB customers historically used Azure Cognitive Search; the cold answer defaulted to that integration rather than the DocumentDB integrated search features now available.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cognitive Search integration common pattern (older guidance)

confusions.build_risk: If a builder plans to implement full-text using an external Cognitive Search, they will add unnecessary complexity and cost instead of using the service's integrated search stage.
improvements: Add a 'When to use integrated $search vs Azure Cognitive Search' short guide on the DocumentDB search docs to prevent builders defaulting to external indexing.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Cosmos DB's MongoDB API advertises compatibility with specific MongoDB wire protocol versions that vary; historically supported versions included 3.2, 3.6, 4.0, etc. Some features may be limited (server-side JavaScript, some aggregation operators, limited transactions).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0, 6.0, 7.0, and 8.0 and implements ~99% of MongoDB operators; multi-document ACID transactions are supported. There remain a small set of administrative or low-demand aggregation stages and server admin commands that the managed service either abstracts or doesn't expose; the compatibility reference details which operators/stages differ.

grounding_links.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB
Azure DocumentDB at a glance - MongoDB compatibility

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer referenced much older MongoDB compatibility versions (3.x/4.x) and general caveats; the product now supports newer wire protocol versions (5–8).
confusions.build_risk: If a builder relies on MongoDB features added in recent server versions and doesn't confirm the cluster's declared server version, they might use unsupported operators. Always check the cluster's supported wire protocol and run the compatibility assessment if migrating.
improvements: Call out supported wire protocol versions prominently in the quickstart and driver guidance pages; provide a short migration checklist for driver version compatibility.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: There is an Azure Cosmos DB emulator for the SQL API, but it does NOT fully support the MongoDB API. For MongoDB API development you either use the live cloud cluster or run a local MongoDB server (mongo:latest). Cosmos DB MongoDB API endpoints typically listen on port 10255 for direct TLS connections (or use SRV).
confusions.grounded_answer: You can run the open-source DocumentDB gateway locally via the DocumentDB Docker image; the gateway listens on port 10260 by default for local development (examples and quickstarts show docker run with -p 10260:10260 and mongodb://localhost:10260/?tls=true&tlsAllowInvalidCertificates=true).

grounding_links.title: Tutorial: Build a TypeScript app with DocumentDB and deploy to Azure DocumentDB (local Docker gateway port 10260)
Quickstart: Evaluate DocumentDB on Azure Local (preview) (port-forward 10260)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer mixed older emulator limitations (Cosmos SQL emulator) and generic advice to use local MongoDB; the DocumentDB open-source gateway Docker image is available and documented.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming no local gateway exists could force builders to test only against the live cluster; that's acceptable but slower. The local gateway (10260) is convenient for fast iteration.
improvements: Add an explicit 'local development' quickstart that highlights the Docker image and the default port (10260) so builders can easily run a local gateway.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Cosmos DB exposes a change feed for the SQL model; for MongoDB API, native MongoDB change streams are not always available; use the Cosmos DB change feed or other integrations.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB change streams. For multishard clusters, there is a feature toggle (Change streams for multishard clusters) that must be enabled (a portal 'Features' switch) in some configurations; single-shard change streams work normally. The docs describe enabling change streams for multishard clusters and show example code.

grounding_links.title: Change streams in Azure DocumentDB
Mongoose on Azure DocumentDB (Model.watch uses change streams guidance)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Confusion between Cosmos DB change feed (SQL API) and the MongoDB change stream API; the vCore DocumentDB product implements MongoDB-style change streams (with a multishard feature flag for cross-shard streaming).
confusions.build_risk: Assuming change streams are unavailable would prevent using Model.watch() and would complicate online migration or reactive features unnecessarily.
improvements: Add a short note in the change-streams doc explaining when the multishard feature toggle is required and how to enable it (portal 'Features' page).

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Expect an MCP server named for the service (e.g. 'documentdb') to provide dedicated data-plane tooling; the generic Azure MCP server may not include MongoDB-specific inspection/agent commands. In practice, use the 'documentdb' MCP server/tools (if available) to inspect collections and indexes.
confusions.grounded_answer: This is correct: the 'documentdb' MCP server provides dedicated data-plane tools for the service (list_databases, aggregate, create_index, explain_operation, etc.). The generic 'azure' MCP server is present for control-plane tasks but does not substitute for the specialized documentdb data-plane tools.
confusions.grounding_source: machine inventory (documentdb MCP server) and learn docs

grounding_links.title: documentdb (MCP server) tool listing (inventory)
Azure DocumentDB MCP Toolkit

confusions.build_risk: None — the inventory shows the documentdb MCP server is available and should be used for data-plane verification.

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically Microsoft used the name 'DocumentDB' for the original document database service which evolved into Azure Cosmos DB (DocumentDB was the SQL API). 'Azure DocumentDB' was essentially the precursor name of Cosmos DB's document model. The open-source 'DocumentDB' (if referenced elsewhere) is unrelated; the Microsoft DocumentDB name was the original Microsoft product name.
confusions.grounded_answer: There is real cause for confusion: the original Azure 'DocumentDB' name was used historically for the early Cosmos DB SQL engine; more recently Microsoft introduced a product named 'Azure DocumentDB' (vCore, MongoDB-compatible) which is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine (the open-source project 'DocumentDB' exists). Also, older Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore) branding has been used — the right relationship is: the new managed product (often called 'Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)') is a first-party Azure service built on the open-source DocumentDB engine and is distinct from Amazon DocumentDB and the older Cosmos DB RU-based MongoDB API.

grounding_links.title: Moving from another MongoDB-compatible service to Azure DocumentDB
Azure DocumentDB at a glance

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The product and brand names have evolved (DocumentDB → Cosmos DB → new Azure DocumentDB vCore), leading to overlaps in historical references and docs.
confusions.build_risk: A builder who confuses this may consult the wrong docs (Cosmos RU-based guidance) or pick wrong CLI/resource types.
improvements: Add a concise 'naming and lineage' note in the overview pages clarifying the differences between 'Azure DocumentDB (vCore)', 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU)', and the historical 'DocumentDB' name.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: For the MongoDB API the data plane is Cosmos DB's implementation that speaks the MongoDB wire protocol — it is not necessarily a vanilla MongoDB server under the hood. That means most driver-level code (queries, indexes) works, but some server-specific features/behaviors differ (indexing semantics, some aggregation stages, transactions and server commands).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore) is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine (the project 'documentdb'), which Microsoft open-sourced. The service implements the MongoDB wire protocol for compatibility, so most MongoDB driver code works; however builders should consult the compatibility reference. The engine being DocumentDB (not a vanilla MongoDB server) means some administrative commands and a small set of operators are different or abstracted by the platform.

grounding_links.title: DocumentDB: The Open-Source Engine Powering Azure DocumentDB
Why migrate to Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described the Cosmos DB-backed MongoDB API; the vCore DocumentDB product is instead powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine and implements MongoDB-compatible APIs.
confusions.build_risk: If a builder assumes a plain MongoDB server or a Cosmos RU backend, they may rely on admin commands or behaviors that the DocumentDB engine doesn't support.
improvements: Add a single line on the main 'overview' that the service runs the open-source DocumentDB engine and point to the compatibility and operator lists so developers test their specific features.

confusions.question: What connection string format will the sample's Mongoose code expect in DOCUMENTDB_URI?
confusions.cold_answer: Expect a MongoDB URI that Mongoose accepts, e.g. either SRV or direct form: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<host>:10255/sample_customer_360_06?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false
confusions.grounded_answer: The sample should accept a standard MongoDB URI but the vCore Azure DocumentDB clusters typically provide SRV-style URIs (mongodb+srv://<username>@<cluster>.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?tls=true&authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256&retrywrites=false). Builders should read connection strings from the portal or az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings and pass the URI unchanged to mongoose.connect().

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using Azure portal (SRV example)
az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used legacy Cosmos-style port 10255 and replicaSet=globaldb; the vCore product uses a different host suffix and SRV patterns. Both forms are 'MongoDB-compatible' but the exact host/ports differ by product.

confusion_sources.title: Cosmos DB MongoDB connection string docs (older)

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong host/port/params will cause connection failure or TLS/auth issues; the builder should not hard-code port 10255 in the .env.example and should instead instruct 'put the connection string as given by the portal or az documentdb list-connection-strings'.
improvements: In the sample's .env.example, show a placeholder SRV form (mongodb+srv://<username>@<cluster>.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com) and a brief note: 'Use the connection string from the Azure portal or az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings'.

confusions.question: How should the sample implement paginated history and channel-breakdown aggregation endpoints?
confusions.cold_answer: Pagination: implement time-based or cursor pagination using the timestamp index (e.g. query by customerId and timestamp < lastSeenTimestamp, limit N). Avoid large skip; use range queries on timestamp + limit. Channel breakdown: use an aggregation pipeline to $match by customerId (and time range), then $group by channel and $count.
confusions.grounded_answer: This is correct: use cursor/time-based pagination leveraging the {customerId:1, timestamp:-1} index (e.g., query by customerId and timestamp < lastSeenTimestamp, limit N, or use compound cursor on timestamp + _id for stable ordering). Channel breakdown is implemented with an aggregation: $match (filters) then $group: { _id: "$channel", count: { $sum: 1 } } — the (channel,timestamp) index supports time-bounded channel queries.

grounding_links.title: Index patterns and query cookbook (documentdb-indexing)
Pagination and range queries guidance (examples)

confusions.build_risk: None — this is the recommended approach and aligns with the requested compound indexes.

information_gaps.title: Mongoose version compatibility
information_gaps.description: Which exact Mongoose (and underlying mongodb driver) version should the sample pin for Node.js 24 to guarantee compatibility with MongoDB wire protocol 7.0/8.0 on the target cluster? I searched Microsoft Learn and the installed skills but did not find a concrete 'recommended Mongoose version for wire protocol X' statement.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use the mongoClusters resource type (Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters) and az documentdb mongocluster CLI group — do not use Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts or az cosmosdb for vCore DocumentDB clusters.

Read the cluster connection string from the portal or run az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings and pass that exact URI (SRV form is common) to mongoose.connect(); do not hard-code port 10255 or replicaSet=globaldb as those are for older Cosmos DB endpoints.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Provision/expect capacity using the cluster tier (vCores) and storage (e.g., M30), not request units; size test workloads accordingly.

inventory_recommendations.name: azd
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not necessary for this sample: the cluster is pre-provisioned and az is available for control-plane inspection. If IaC via azd is desired in future, install Azure Developer CLI (azd) using Microsoft instructions.

inventory_recommendations.name: bicep
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this sample because no provisioning is needed; if the team wants to include Bicep templates for reproducible infra, install Bicep CLI (az bicep install) or rely on az CLI's bicep integration.

inventory_recommendations.name: terraform
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required to build this sample; include Terraform only if the user wants an alternate IaC flow. To add it, install Terraform per HashiCorp instructions or use AzAPI provider modules for mongoClusters.

inventory_recommendations.name: dotnet
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for a Node.js Mongoose sample. Add only if you plan cross-language samples.

inventory_recommendations.name: mongosh
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Useful for quick manual checks (insert, find, index inspection). Install mongosh on PATH (download from mongodb.com) or use npx mongosh. Workaround: use the documentdb MCP server tools (documentdb_find_documents, documentdb_list_indexes) or a short Node script using the MongoDB driver to perform manual checks.
